passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Washing Machine Out of Warranty

emails.subject: Model HW-620, serial 4471882 — bearing failure at 26 months
emails.body:
Dear Halden Support,

I bought an HW-620 washing machine on 14 August two years ago for $899. The drum bearing failed last week, at 26 months. Your warranty is 24 months, so I understand the warranty answer is no.

I am writing anyway, for two reasons.

First, your engineer told me the bearing is not sold separately and that the entire drum assembly must be replaced at $610 plus labour. On a $899 machine that is not a repair, it is a decision to buy a new one. I would like to know whether that is deliberate design or simply how the part is supplied, because those are different things and only one of them is your choice.

Second, I checked before writing: your own marketing describes this range as "built for a decade of family washing". I am not claiming that is a contractual promise. I am saying that if a machine is sold on a ten-year expectation and the main bearing fails at just over two, one of those two numbers is wrong and it is not the one I chose.

I am not demanding a free repair. I would like a straight answer on the part, and I would like to know what you consider a reasonable life for this machine.

Regards,
Emeka Balogun

emails.subject: RE: Model HW-620, serial 4471882 — bearing failure at 26 months
emails.body:
Dear Mr Balogun,

Two straight answers, then an offer you did not ask for.

On the part: the bearing is pressed into the drum assembly and is not separately serviceable on the HW-620. That is a design decision, not a supply accident, and it was made to reduce manufacturing cost. I am not going to describe it as anything else. Our current range separates the two, and that change was made because of complaints like yours.

On reasonable life: our internal design target for this range is eight to ten years for the machine and seven for the bearing. Yours failed at just over two. That is not normal wear and it is not something you did.

Which brings me to the offer. Because the failure is well outside the expected distribution, this goes to our engineering team as a warranty-adjacent case regardless of the 24-month term. We will replace the drum assembly at no charge for the part; you would pay the standard labour call-out of $95. That is not goodwill, it is what the failure data supports.

On the marketing copy: you are right that "a decade of family washing" sits badly beside a two-year bearing failure. I have passed it to the team that owns it. I cannot promise it will change, and I would rather say that than tell you it will.

Regards,
Joanna Petrescu
Customer Support Lead

passages.title: Why Things Are Harder to Repair Than They Were
passages.content:
The perception that appliances and electronics do not last as they once did is widely held and only partly accurate. Some products genuinely fail sooner. Others last as long as ever and have simply become uneconomic to fix, which produces the same experience for the owner and has an entirely different cause.

The most common barrier is not a conspiracy to make things break. It is that repair has become expensive relative to replacement, and that ratio moved for reasons that had nothing to do with durability. Manufacturing costs fell steeply as production scaled and automated; skilled labour costs did not. A repair requiring an hour of a trained technician's time can therefore exceed the price of a new unit assembled in minutes, even when the fault is trivial and the rest of the product is sound.

Design choices then compound it. Components bonded rather than fastened, batteries glued into housings, and sub-assemblies sold only as complete modules all raise the cost of the smallest repair. These decisions usually have defensible engineering justifications — bonding saves space and improves water resistance, and modules reduce assembly errors. They also have the effect, whether intended or not, of turning a five-dollar failure into a hundred-dollar one.

Information is a quieter barrier and often the decisive one. Where service manuals, diagnostic software and error-code documentation are restricted to authorised networks, an independent technician who is perfectly capable of the physical repair cannot identify the fault or reset the system afterwards. The part may be available and the skill may exist; the repair still cannot happen. Several jurisdictions have legislated on precisely this point, which is a reasonable indication of where the practical obstacle sits.

The evidence on deliberate shortening of product life is thinner than the public discussion suggests. Documented cases exist and are genuinely egregious, but they are a small share of the problem. The larger share is the ordinary result of cost pressure, engineering trade-offs and restricted information, none of which requires anyone to have decided that a product should fail.

That distinction matters because it points at different remedies. Outrage addresses sabotage. What the evidence supports is duller and more effective: mandated parts availability, published repair documentation, and design standards that keep the cheapest failure from requiring the most expensive fix.

passages.title: Should Manufacturers Be Required to Supply Spare Parts?

viewpoints.name: Minister Halima Osei
viewpoints.text: We legislated parts availability and I would do it again, though not for the reason usually given. The waste argument is real and it is not what moved the file — what moved it was that consumers could not get a price. Before the rule, a manufacturer could decline to supply and the owner had no way to know whether repair was impossible or merely unoffered. The rule forces that into the open. Whether it extends average product life by a measurable amount, I genuinely do not know yet, and anyone quoting a figure is ahead of the data.

viewpoints.name: Sunniva Dahl, appliance manufacturer
viewpoints.text: We support parts availability and we already exceeded the requirement before it existed. My objection is the ten-year stocking obligation applied identically to a company our size and to one with forty times the turnover. Warehousing slow-moving parts for a decade is a fixed cost that scales badly downward, and the effect at the margin is fewer small manufacturers, not more repairable products. Set the obligation against revenue and you get the same outcome without consolidating the market.

viewpoints.name: Idris Vaughan, independent repair technician
viewpoints.text: Parts were never my main obstacle and I say that as someone the rule was written for. I can source parts. What I cannot source is the diagnostic software and the authorisation code to pair a replacement component to the machine. A part I can fit and cannot commission is not a repair. The legislation solved the visible half of the problem and left the half that actually stops me working, and I suspect that is because parts are easy to photograph and software access is not.

viewpoints.name: Professor Nadia Ferreira, environmental economist
viewpoints.text: I support the policy and the environmental case for it is weaker than campaigners state. Extending the life of an appliance reduces manufacturing emissions and, for anything that consumes energy in use, keeps a less efficient unit running longer. For a fridge or a washing machine the balance depends on how much efficiency has improved since it was made, and sometimes replacement is genuinely the lower-carbon choice. The durable argument for repair is consumer autonomy and cost, not carbon, and I would rather it were argued there.
